_comment_story_merge: The story-merge family -- cmd_story_merge, _story_merge_resolve_axis and the three writers -- captured the same way, before its jq was deleted: 92 cases over one adversarial corpus spanning legacy mode, both split axes, --foundation, --phase-aware, --agent-mode, and the write failures nobody had exercised. Recorded per case: the flags, the staging files it was handed (`input`, so the case is REPLAYABLE and not merely described), exit code, stdout, stderr, every file left under .aimi/tasks with its content, and the whole .aimi tree listing, so a refusal that wrote something as a side effect could not hide. Each case ran in its own throwaway project root; paths are relative because the flags were; createdAt normalizes to <DATE> (it is today's date by construction), mktemp's six random characters to <MKTEMP> (that one SURVIVED is the evidence, not which one), and the absolute script path and line number a shell diagnostic quotes to <CLI> and <N>. Two runs of the pre-port CLI produce this file byte for byte. 440 of 460 field comparisons identical after the port -- every stdout, stderr, written file and tree matched in 84 of the 92 cases, including every case the 41 black-box calls in the bash suite drive. The 20 that differ fall in 8 cases and are ALL of one kind: jq or `set -e` aborting before the code's own diagnostic could run, so the exit status was the engine's and the message the code was written to print was unreachable. They are named here so nobody has to rediscover them. (1) arquivo-array, the loud one: a staging file holding an ARRAY of stories, which the story-merge docs promise is supported. The bash has a complete flattening loop for it, introduced with the comment 'Simpler approach: just append with sequential indices' -- and directly above that loop a first attempt calling `path` with no argument, which is a compile error, whose 2>/dev/null'd failure assigned the EMPTY STRING over the accumulator the loop was about to append to. jq then aborted (exit 5, 'null (null) has no keys') and nothing was ever written. The Python runs the loop the bash was written to run, so an array file now merges. This is the one recorded difference that is a capability rather than a message, and it is deliberate: writing code to reproduce a swallowed compile error would be writing the defect on purpose. (2) json-numero and json-string (exit 5 -> 1): a staging file whose top-level value is a number or a string. jq aborted adding it to {_srcIdx}; the Python refuses by name and says which file. (3) json-multiplos-valores (exit 2 -> 1): two JSON values in one file. `jq -e .` accepted it and `--argjson` rejected it three steps later; the Python reports it at the malformed-JSON check, which is where that question was already being asked. (4) dep-nao-string (exit 5 -> 1): a dependsOn entry that is not a string. jq aborted in startswith(); the Python lets it through the outline remap, and Kahn's algorithm reports it as a cycle -- which is what the bash already did for every other dependsOn naming no story, and is preserved on purpose. (5) escrita-legada-falha and side-escrita-falha: a directory where the lock file goes. `set -e` killed the shell on the failing `200>` redirect, so the legacy and SIDE writers' own 'failed to write output file' branch was unreachable dead code and the mktemp scratch file survived. The Python prints that message and removes the scratch file. Both remain refusals at exit 1 that write no tasks file, which the file and tree fields confirm. (6) proj-falha-parcial: the same obstacle on the PROJECT axis, where `|| write_exit=$?` kept the branch reachable. Its whole three-set report is byte-identical; the only difference is the shell's own redirect diagnostic, which preceded it and has no Python equivalent.

_comment_tasks_read: The six read-only tasks.json verbs -- status (both branches), metadata, get-story, current-story, get-state and count-pending -- captured the same way, before their jq was deleted: 151 cases over one adversarial corpus, at commit 9716146. Recorded per case: the argv, the tasks file the run was given and the .aimi/state/ files it started with (`input`, so the case is REPLAYABLE and not merely described), exit code, stdout, stderr, and every .aimi/ file left behind afterwards (`state_after`), so a read-only verb that wrote something as a side effect could not hide -- 19 cases legitimately leave one, and those recordings are the evidence that get_tasks_file's stale-state self-heal and its .state.lock still run in bash. Each case ran in its own throwaway project root; exactly one normalization rule fired, the temp root to /TMP, and nothing else in the recording is non-deterministic: two runs of the pre-port CLI produce this file byte for byte. The corpus is weighted toward inputs the schema does not allow, because that is the only place jq and Python can differ -- the maxConcurrency value space on all three former call sites (absent, null, false, true, 0, 0.0, -1, -0.5, 20.0, 20.5, 999999, a string, an array, an object), metadata absent / null / {} / a string / an array / a number, userStories absent / null / [] / an object / a string across five verbs, a story that is null and a story that is a string, dependsOn null / false / a string, priority as 1.0, an unknown story id, a duplicated story id, a current-story pointer that is unset / empty / stale / never validated, no tasks file at all, a stale current-tasks pointer, the nested phase-folder layout, and seven whole-document shapes (malformed, empty, null, an array, a number, a string, two concatenated values). 530 of 604 field comparisons identical after the port -- every stdout and every state_after matched in all 151 cases, and 114 of the 151 matched on all four fields. Every clamp case is byte-identical on all three call sites, which is the thing this slice existed to prove: `true` still clamps to 20 because jq orders booleans below numbers so `true <= 0` holds, 0 and 0.0 still clamp because jq's `//` treats both as present, 20.0 still renders as 20 rather than 20.0, and a string, an array or an object still passes through UNCHANGED because jq orders those above numbers and the comparison is simply false -- the case a naive Python `value <= 0` raises TypeError on. The 74 fields that differ fall in 37 cases, are exit code and stderr only, and are ALL of one kind: jq aborting mid-expression, so the exit status was the engine's (5 for a runtime error, 4 for a parse error) and the message the code would otherwise have printed did not exist. Every one of them was, and still is, a refusal that writes nothing to stdout; only the wording and the number moved, to `Error: <verb>: <file>: <expression>: <what went wrong>` at exit 1. Recorded rather than reproduced: synthesizing an engine error would be the only way to match, and that is not a thing to write on purpose -- same shape as the nine named in _comment_lifecycle. They cluster into five classes, and KNOWN_DIVERGENCES in test_tasks.py names all 37 individually. (1) userStories absent, null, an object or a string: 16 cases across status, status --counts-only, count-pending and current-story (`status-us-*`, `counts-us-*`, `count-pending-us-*`, `current-story-us-*`), all of them jq's 'Cannot iterate over null' or 'Cannot iterate over string'. get-story is NOT among them -- validate_story_exists still runs in bash and refuses first, so all five of its us-* cases are byte-identical, which is what keeping that gate out of Python bought. (2) metadata a string, an array or a number: 4 cases (`meta-string`, `meta-array`, `meta-numero`, `status-meta-string`), jq's 'Cannot index ... with string'. (3) a whole document that is not an object: 13 cases (`doc-json-array-*`, `doc-json-numero-*`, `doc-json-string-*`, `doc-json-null-status`, `doc-json-null-count`, `doc-json-dois-valores-status`, `doc-json-dois-valores-count`). doc-json-null-METADATA is deliberately not among them: jq's assignment onto null BUILDS the object, so a null document still yields {"maxConcurrency": 20}, and the port does the same. (4) malformed JSON: 3 cases (`doc-json-malformado-*`), jq's own parse error at exit 4. (5) a story that is not an object: 1 case (`historia-nao-objeto`). A story that is NULL is deliberately not among them -- jq indexes null happily and emits a row of nulls, which the port reproduces. Two jq behaviours that have nothing to do with the tasks schema were preserved rather than tidied away, and both are byte-identical here. An EMPTY tasks file makes jq read zero values from its input stream, so the verb prints nothing and exits 0 (`doc-json-vazio-*`, 3 cases): a truncated write reports success, which is a silent hole, ranked and left alone because a port is not where a defect is fixed. And a file holding two concatenated documents runs the verb once per document (`doc-json-dois-valores-metadata`, which prints two objects). tasks.py's read_docs reads the same stream for both reasons; a plain json.load would have broken four otherwise-identical cases to no one's benefit.

_comment_tasks_ready: list-ready (plain and --brief), next-story, and the bash validate_story_exists gate the get-story arm of it runs -- captured the same way as tasks_read_cases and for the same reason: 128 cases over one adversarial corpus, at commit cfbc7c2, BEFORE the jq was deleted. Recorded per case: the argv, the tasks file the run was given and the .aimi/ state it started with (`input`, so every case is REPLAYABLE and not merely described), exit code, stdout, stderr, and every .aimi/ file left behind (`state_after`) -- which matters more here than it did for the read verbs, because next-story WRITES current-story, and 47 cases leave one. Each case ran in its own throwaway project root; exactly one normalization rule fired, the temp root to /TMP. 451 of 512 field comparisons are identical after the port: every stdout and every state_after matched in all 128 cases, and 91 of the 128 matched on all four fields. THE FOUR ORDERING AND PREDICATE TRAPS, each with the case that pins it. (1) jq's sort_by is STABLE, so stories tied on priority keep tasks.json file order -- `empate` lists US-007, US-003, US-009 all at priority 5 in that file order and next-story picks US-007, which is the determinism /aimi:execute documents. (2) jq's total order puts null BELOW every number, so a story whose priority is null or absent is picked FIRST, ahead of priority 1 -- `prioridade-nula` picks the null one over priority 1, `prioridade-ausente` picks the absent one over the null one on file order, and the `ordem-*` ladder walks the rest of the order one class boundary at a time (false below 0 and true, true below every number, a number below a string, a string below an array, an array below an object). Intra-class comparison of two arrays or two objects is deliberately NOT in the corpus: roadmap.py's jq_sort_key ranks all arrays equal where jq would compare them elementwise, and a priority that is an array is not a thing -- the boundary is named here rather than papered over. (3) jq's `all` ends at the first element whose condition selected NOTHING and answers true, which is stronger than 'a dangling dependsOn id does not block'. `dep-pendurada-antes` is the case that shows it: US-002 depends on [US-999, US-001] and is READY even though US-001 carries a pending action gate, while US-003 depends on [US-001, US-999] -- the same two ids, other order -- and is blocked. A port that treated a dangling id as merely vacuous would agree on the first and silently drop the second from the wave. `dep-pendurada` and `dep-pendurada-duplicada` cover the rest of that walk, including a dependsOn id that matches TWO stories, where either match can block. (4) --brief emits exactly six keys, id/title/priority/dependsOn/project/gate, because jq's object-construction shorthand writes a key holding null for a field the story does not have -- `pronta-sem-campos-brief` is a story carrying none of the four optional ones and it still yields six. dependsOn there is the RAW field, null and all: the `// []` belongs to the predicate, not to the projection. The corpus is otherwise weighted toward inputs the schema does not allow, because that is the only place jq and Python can differ: every gate kind and status on the story itself and on a dependency, every story status as a dependency, dependsOn as null / false / 0 / "" / {} / an object of values / a string / a number / true, a story that is null and a story that is a string, userStories absent / null / [] / an object / a string, and seven whole-document shapes. Two jq quirks that decide readiness are preserved rather than tidied and are recorded in `depende-formas`, where all of them are stories the pre-port CLI listed as READY: `//` leaves 0, "" and {} alone (none of them is null or false), and jq's `length` then gives a number its ABSOLUTE VALUE and a string its codepoints, so `dependsOn: 0` and `dependsOn: ""` both have length 0 and short-circuit the dependency walk exactly as [] does. tasks.py's jq_length is that rule; a plain len() would abort on the first and mis-answer the second. The 61 fields that differ fall in 37 cases and are exit code and stderr only. Twelve document shapes abort mid-expression, and each contributes three cases that split by VERB rather than by input: `-ready` and `-brief` surfaced jq's abort as the CLI's own exit status (5 for a runtime error, 4 for a parse error) and now refuse at exit 1 with `Error: <verb>: <file>: <expression>: <what went wrong>`, while `-next` answered `null` at exit 0 with the pointer cleared and STILL DOES -- only the wording on stderr moved. The twelve are dependsOn as a string / a number / true, a gate that is a string on the story or on a dependency, a story that is a string, userStories absent / null / a string, a document that is null / an array, and malformed JSON. The 37th is `sem-arquivo-next`, its own class: nothing aborted, jq was simply handed an empty filename after get_tasks_file had already refused and complained a second time about it, so the port prints one line where the recording has two. All 37 are named individually in READY_DIVERGENCES in test_tasks.py, and test_each_excused_ready_case_keeps_its_answer holds each to its ANSWER: a refusal still refuses and writes nothing to stdout, and a null still clears the pointer and exits 0. Two behaviours that have nothing to do with the tasks schema are preserved rather than evened out. An EMPTY tasks file makes the verb produce no output at all, and the pre-port code then printed a bare newline without --brief (`result=$(jq ...)` then `echo "$result"`) and nothing with it (that newline was piped through a second jq, which read it as no input): `doc-vazio-ready` records "\n" and `doc-vazio-brief` records "", and cmd_list_ready keeps the two branches apart to reproduce it. And next-story has always SWALLOWED every failure beneath it -- cmd_list_ready ran on the left of a pipeline inside a command substitution, so neither its exit for a missing tasks file nor jq's abort on a malformed one ever reached the caller; the empty result cleared current-story and printed null at exit 0. /aimi:next reads that null as 'all stories complete' and stops, so the swallow is now written down as `|| story=""` instead of being an accident of pipeline structure. Neither is fixed here: a port is not where a defect gets settled.

WHERE A NAIVE PYTHON WOULD HAVE DIVERGED, each with the recorded case that catches it: `unique` inside validate-deps' cycle reduce sorts a dependsOn holding null, a number and a string, which jq orders and Python's sorted() raises TypeError on (deps-heterogeneo, the one place in these four that needs roadmap.py's jq_sort_key); `==` says a boolean is not a number, so a hand-edited `wave: true` IS a mismatch against a computed 0 where Python's `1 == True` would have hidden it (wave-true); `jq -r` unquotes a string and pretty-prints everything else, so an id that is `[1, 2]` reaches bash's line-at-a-time loop as FOUR lines and yields four errors from one story (id-array), while an id containing a newline yields two well-formed ids from one story (id-newline) and an id that is the empty string is skipped entirely and not even counted (id-vazio). Two whole-file behaviours were preserved rather than tidied away. An EMPTY tasks file makes jq read zero values, and the three verbs that piped their output through `echo` therefore print a BLANK LINE and refuse (doc-vazio-deps and doc-vazio-stories at exit 1), while validate-ids answers `{valid: true, count: 0}` and validate-waves prints nothing at all, both at exit 0. And a file holding TWO concatenated documents runs each verb twice: validate-deps then exits 1 even when both documents are valid, because its status came from comparing two lines of `.valid` against the one word `true` (dois-documentos-validos-deps), while validate-stories' `jq -e` reported on the LAST document alone and validate-ids pooled both documents' ids into a single verdict.

_comment_validate_tasks: validate-tasks -- cmd_validate_tasks plus its two spec helpers, ~290 lines and the largest single function in this port -- captured exactly the way the four blocks before it were, and before its jq was deleted: 121 cases at commit 3350206. Recorded per case: the argv, the tasks file the run was given, the PROJECT_ROOT-relative spec fixtures on disk (`files`), the fixtures written OUTSIDE the project root (`outside`, one directory up) and the .aimi/state/ files it started with -- `input`, so every case is REPLAYABLE rather than merely described -- then exit code, stdout, stderr and every .aimi/ file left behind (`state_after`). All 121 `state_after` values are empty and that is this block's own evidence: validate-tasks is a pure reader, takes no lock, writes no temp file and touches no document, so a port that started writing one would have nowhere to hide. Each case ran in its own throwaway root; three normalizations fired (the root to /TMP, its parent to /OUT, the CLI's own path to /CLI/aimi-cli.sh) and nothing else in the recording is non-deterministic. 473 of 484 field comparisons identical after the port; 115 of the 121 cases matched on all four fields, and EVERY stdout and EVERY state_after matched in all 121. The 11 fields that differ fall in 6 cases, are exit code and stderr ONLY, and are all of one kind: an ENGINE aborting where no code of ours ran. Five are jq (exit 5 for a runtime error, 4 for a parse error) with its message swallowed by the `2>/dev/null` on the assignment that invoked it, so the pre-port recording shows an exit status and an EMPTY stderr; ds-ac-null and aborta-antes-das-regras-finais are to_entries against a null acceptanceCriteria, historias-ausente is `.userStories[]` against an absent userStories, metadata-string is indexing a metadata that is a string, and json-malformado is jq's own parse error at its own exit 4. Each is now a refusal that writes nothing to stdout, at `Error: validate-tasks: <file>: <expression>: <what went wrong>` and exit 1 -- only the wording and the number moved. The sixth, dois-documentos-endpoints, is not jq at all: `endpoint_count` was one jq run over the WHOLE stream, so a file holding two documents handed bash two numbers on two lines and `[ "$ep_index" -lt "$endpoint_count" ]` refused them, printing bash's own `[: 1\n2: integer expression expected` naming aimi-cli.sh line 10430 -- a line number in a function that no longer exists. _comment_story_context: get-story-context -- cmd_get_story_context, 155 lines of bash running 8 fixed jq calls plus one per skill, captured exactly the way the five blocks before it were and before its bash was deleted: 57 cases at commit bdaa0ad. THE VERB EVERY SPAWNED STORY EXECUTOR RUNS FIRST, which is why its SHAPE is recorded case by case rather than described -- a downstream agent silently receiving an empty payload, or a key it did not expect, shows up as a confused agent and never as a red test. Recorded per case: the argv, the tasks file, the fixtures on disk (`files` verbatim, `repeat` as [unit, count] or [unit, count, prefix] so a 100KB skill costs the golden a line instead of 100KB), whether AIMI_PLUGIN_DIR was exported (`plugin_dir`, the only way to point _resolve_skills_base_dir at a fixture), the environment overrides (`env` -- LC_ALL, for the two multibyte twins) and the .aimi/state/ files it started with -- `input`, so every case is REPLAYABLE rather than merely described -- then exit code, stdout, stderr and every .aimi/ file left behind (`state_after`). All 57 `state_after` values are empty and that is this block's own evidence: get-story-context is a pure reader, takes no lock, writes no temp file and touches no document. Each case ran in its own throwaway root; three normalizations fired (the root to /TMP, the CLI's own path to /CLI/aimi-cli.sh, and a run-length collapse of any run of 256+ identical characters to `<<c*N>>`, applied to BOTH sides of every comparison so the cap fixtures cost kilobytes instead of a megabyte) and nothing else in the recording is non-deterministic -- two consecutive full captures were byte-identical. THIS CAPTURE PROVES LESS THAN THE FIVE BEFORE IT AND THE TEST MODULE SAYS SO: this function's logic was bash arrays and a shell loop rather than a jq program, so the recording pins payload SHAPE and the hand-written tests, not the corpus, carry the fidelity argument here. 48 of the 57 cases are identical after the port on all four fields, once the new skillsDropped key is removed from the actual stdout -- everything else, key order included, matches byte for byte. THE 9 THAT DIFFER SPLIT IN TWO GROUPS, and the second is not an excuse. GROUP ONE -- SIX ABORTS, NO CODE OF OURS RAN, and three of them are findings rather than trivia. (a) skill-vazio and skill-so-newlines: an EMPTY SKILL.md returned exit 1 with an empty stdout AND an empty stderr -- the agent got nothing at all, with no diagnostic anywhere. `(( skill_aggregate_chars += ${#skill_content} ))` evaluates to the new total, `((expr))` returns 1 when that total is 0, and `set -e` killed the verb; a skill file that is empty (or holds only newlines, which the command substitution strips to empty) triggers it only while the running total is still zero, which is to say when it is declared FIRST. skill-vazio-depois is the control: the same empty file declared second is harmless and matches byte for byte. The port emits it with `content: ""`. (b) brainstorm-truncagem-64k: exit 141, SIGPIPE. `head -c 65536` closes the pipe and `set -o pipefail` promotes the signal, so the 64KB truncation that pipeline was written for is UNREACHABLE -- anything large enough to reach it kills the verb first, and around the pipe-buffer boundary it is not even deterministic (70000 bytes gave exit 0 and exit 141 on the same host in the same minute; the recorded case uses 200000, which was stable across runs). The port truncates at 65536 bytes as the pipeline intended. (c) bundle-string, metadata-string and arquivo-vazio are jq's own message at jq's own exit 5, each now `Error: get-story-context: <file>: <expression>: <what went wrong>` at exit 1 -- only the wording and the number moved, and metadata-string is recorded with the BRAINSTORM read's message rather than the bundle's because the port keeps bash's evaluation order. GROUP TWO -- THE THREE RULES THAT CHANGED ON PURPOSE. (1) THE CAP COUNTS BYTES. cap-multibyte-c and cap-multibyte-c-utf-8 are the same input through the same CLI under two locales and they disagree, which is the whole argument: `${#skill_content}` counted bytes under LC_ALL=C (102600 for a 34200-character body of em-dashes, over the cap, so the reverse-pop loop drained pequeno and mb and then aborted at the zero total -- exit 1, no payload) and characters under LC_ALL=C.UTF-8 (34200, under the cap, both skills kept). The SKILL.md files in this repo are full of em-dashes and arrows, so the divergence was real and reachable rather than theoretical. Both locales now answer identically. Python's len() on a str counts characters and would have been no more faithful than the other reading, so this is a decision, not a translation: a payload cap defends a payload, and a payload is bytes. (2) A SKILL WHOSE OWN BODY EXCEEDS THE CAP IS DROPPED UP FRONT, before the aggregate loop, with its own warning naming it and its size. cap-gigante-primeiro records what that replaces: [oversized, small, small] drained the whole array from the end -- three warnings, the two legitimate skills lost first -- and then aborted the verb at the same zero total, so the caller got nothing. Post-port the oversized one is dropped and both small ones survive, which is what makes declaration order priority order. (3) skillsDropped[] IS EMITTED, always, `[]` when nothing was dropped, each entry {name, bytes, reason} with reason `oversized` or `aggregate`. The warnings stay on stderr where they were -- stdout is parsed by every consumer there is -- but a caller running this verb with 2>/dev/null could not previously tell a hydrated skill set from a halved one. THE AGGREGATE CAP ITSELF IS UNCHANGED AND THAT IS CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: cap-tres-40k (three 40KB skills, gama evicted from the end), cap-fronteira-exata (102400 bytes exactly, nothing evicted, because the test is `>` and not `>=`) and cap-fronteira-mais-um (one byte over, beta evicted) all match byte for byte, warning wording included. THE CORPUS EXERCISES THE SHAPES A CONSUMER BRANCHES ON, which is the anti-vacuum half. Skills: sem-skills and skills-vazio both give `[]`; skills-tres hydrates three in declaration order; skill-ausente reports `skill <name> not found at skills/<name>/SKILL.md — skipped` on stderr and keeps its two siblings; skill-prefixo-opencode resolves the aimi- prefixed directory OpenCode installs while still reporting the bare path; skills-base-nao-resolvida (no AIMI_PLUGIN_DIR, no CLAUDECODE) gives `[]` with NO warning at all; skill-tag-breakout pins both escapes and their order (the closing form first, or the opening rule would eat its `<` and leave `</…` unescaped); skill-sem-newline-final and every other recording show that `$(sed …)` stripped the trailing newline off every body. What the declared list may hold is pinned too, because `jq -r '.[]' 2>/dev/null` swallowed all of it: skills-string and skills-numero yield NO skills and no complaint, skills-objeto iterates an object to its VALUES, skills-item-null and skills-item-numero look up `skills/null/` and `skills/7/`, skills-item-vazio looks up `skills//SKILL.md`, and skills-item-array records `["alpha"]` pretty-printed by `-r` over three lines and read back by `mapfile` as the three skill names `[`, `  "alpha"` and `]`. skill-nome-travessia records the permissive half deliberately: a declared name of `../fora` is looked up at `skills/../fora/SKILL.md` with no confinement, exactly as bash did, and porting it unchanged keeps this block a record of what the code did rather than of what anyone wished it did. designContext: brainstorm-com-decisoes, brainstorm-sem-secao, brainstorm-arquivo-ausente, brainstorm-null, brainstorm-numero and brainstorm-objeto cover the gate; brainstorm-secao-ate-o-fim, brainstorm-subsecao (a `### ` heading stays INSIDE), brainstorm-heading-sufixado (the match is a prefix, so `## Design Decisions e mais` opens the section) and brainstorm-secao-duplicada (a SECOND `## Design Decisions` does NOT close the section -- awk tested that rule first and `next`ed past the closing one, so the two merge) cover the scanner; brainstorm-espacos-e-brancos pins the per-line whitespace strip and the blank-line removal; brainstorm-absoluto pins that an absolute path is used as given while a relative one is joined onto PROJECT_ROOT, neither of them confined. bundle-completo, bundle-parcial (the three fields default to the literal `(none)`, not to blanks), bundle-vazio (`{}` is two characters, so the gate OPENS on an empty object and prints three `(none)`s), bundle-null and bundle-e-brainstorm cover the other half of designContext. And the document itself: metadata-ausente and metadata-null both emit `metadata: null` rather than omitting the key; id-duplicado emits the WHOLE payload twice because `select` is a filter over a stream and not a lookup; dois-documentos takes its story and metadata from the first document while the skills read ran over both; json-malformado is refused by bash's own validate_story_exists before Python is reached at all, as are historia-inexistente, id-invalido and sem-argumento.

The lock's own suffix is computed independently of the task's, so the two only stay paired by coincidence. One rule, two implementations, already disagreeing before any port -- ranked, not fixed here. (5) THE `[ -z "$non_terminal" ]` BRANCH IS REACHED BY EXACTLY ONE INPUT, and it is not the one it reads as if it guards. Under `set -euo pipefail` a jq that FAILS takes the assignment down with it before the test is ever reached, so a document with no userStories (archive-sem-userstories), one whose userStories is a string (archive-userstories-nao-lista) and a malformed one (archive-json-malformado) exit 5, 5 and 4 with EMPTY stderr -- jq's own status, its message swallowed by the 2>/dev/null on the assignment that ran it, and no diagnostic anywhere. The arm fires only for an EMPTY tasks file, where jq exits 0 having printed nothing: archive-arquivo-vazio is refused with the non-terminal message, which is the wrong sentence for the input but is the behaviour. (10) A TWO-DOCUMENT TASKS FILE IS ARCHIVED WHATEVER ITS SECOND DOCUMENT SAYS. jq reads a stream and printed one count per document, so `[ "$non_terminal" -ne 0 ]` was handed "0 1"; `[` reported "integer expression expected" and returned 2, which an `if` reads as FALSE. archive-dois-documentos-um-aberto has an in_progress story in its second document and is archived anyway, with bash's complaint the only trace. (6) validate_path_in_project LETS A NON-EXISTENT TRAVERSAL THROUGH when the parent directory does not exist either: it falls back to the unresolved string, which still starts with PROJECT_ROOT. archive-research-traversal (refused) and archive-research-fora-inexistente (allowed, then skipped as missing) are the same ../fora/... path and differ only in whether fora/ exists. (7) THE TWO CALL-SITE ORDERINGS DIFFER AND BOTH MATTER: researchPaths and prototypePaths are confined BEFORE their existence check, brainstormPath only INSIDE it -- so archive-brainstorm-fora-inexistente is silently skipped where archive-research-fora-inexistente would have been refused had its parent existed. (8) EVERY ESCAPE REFUSAL LANDS AFTER THE TASK FILE AND ITS LOCK HAVE ALREADY MOVED, and after any earlier delete has already happened -- archive-prototype-fora-depois-do-research exits 1 with the task in the archive and .aimi/research/r1.md already gone. A refusal with a side effect is visible in these records because `tree` is compared, and that is the field's whole reason for being here. (9) A DIRECTORY NAMED IN researchPaths ENDS THE RUN MID-ARCHIVE: `rm -f` refuses it, `set -e` does the rest, and archive-research-diretorio exits 1 with the task already archived and the directory and both files under it untouched. Nothing recurses, and nothing in the port may start. AFTER THE PORT: 238 of the 246 field comparisons are identical. Every `file`, every `tree` and every `outside_after` matched in all 41 cases -- which is the half that matters here, because those three ARE the verb: nothing moved that did not move before, nothing was deleted that was not deleted before, and no refusal gained or lost a side effect. The 8 that differ fall in 5 cases and in two classes, neither of them a rule anyone wrote. (A) THE ENGINE'S OWN STATUS WITH NO MESSAGE AT ALL, exit and stderr in archive-sem-userstories, archive-userstories-nao-lista and archive-json-malformado: jq aborted and `set -euo pipefail` took the script down at jq's exit 5, 5 and 4, with jq's message swallowed by the 2>/dev/null on the assignment that ran it, so the recording is of a silent death. tasks.py refuses at 1 with a line naming the verb and the file. Recorded rather than reproduced, exactly as the six blocks before this one did with their engine aborts -- synthesizing an engine error on purpose is not a thing to write -- and all three still refuse, still print nothing to stdout, and still leave the tree exactly as bash left it. (B) BASH'S COMPLAINT ABOUT ITS OWN COMPARISON, stderr only, in archive-dois-documentos and archive-dois-documentos-um-aberto: `[` was handed one count per document, reported "integer expression expected" and returned 2, which the `if` read as false. The port branches on the count instead, so it archives the same file with nothing on stderr. The archive it produces is identical, which is what the tree comparison says; what is gone is a diagnostic that named no rule. _comment_models_read: models.json READERS -- cmd_resolve_models, cmd_get_current_models, cmd_models_prompt_check and cmd_list_models -- captured the way every block before them was, by running the bash and jq still standing in aimi-cli.sh BEFORE a line of it was deleted: 114 cases at commit 9d45ddf. cmd_detect_models is the WRITER of this same file and is NOT here; it is captured with its own block by its own slice. models.json is a GLOBAL file, so every case builds a throwaway config root and points AIMI_CONFIG_DIR and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR at it, and PATH is a shim directory of symlinks rather than the developer's -- nothing here can reach the real ~/.config/aimi/ or ~/.claude/plugins/cache/. `input` is the whole rebuild recipe: `config` is the file's exact bytes (null when there is no file at all, which is a different case from an empty one), `host` is claudeCode (CLAUDECODE=1) or opencode (unset), `opencode_stub` is the script installed on PATH under the name `opencode` (null when the binary is ABSENT, which is a different case again from one that prints nothing), `python3` says whether a python3 symlink was placed in that shim directory, `marker` names the per-host models-prompt-seen-<host> file to pre-create, and `seed_cache` writes models-oc-cache-<mtime>.txt keyed on the CONFIG FILE's own mtime before the run. `files` is every file left in the root afterwards WITH ITS CONTENTS, because _oc_models_cache_path writes a sibling next to models.json and nothing ever collects it -- the same reason archive_cases records a tree. Two normalizations fire, on the way in and on the way out: the root becomes /TMP and the mtime-derived cache filename becomes models-oc-cache-<MTIME>.txt. Without them two captures could not be byte-identical; with them, two consecutive full captures are. THE CORPUS FAILS ON PURPOSE, and here is the roll-call. Accepted: a valid v2.0 config on both hosts, the literal string `inherit`, an id padded with spaces, a config holding only the OTHER host's table. Rejected with the pt-BR string "schema 1.0 obsoleto -- re-rode aimi-cli detect-models", which resolve-models and get-current-models each own a copy of: a real v1.0 document, a v2.0 one carrying a top-level .models key, one with no schemaVersion at all, a bare JSON string, and -- see (3) -- malformed JSON. Warned and degraded to inherit: an unknown id per host, an id with an internal space, an internal tab, a double tab, a backslash, a newline. Silently absent: an empty string, a null, a false, an absent `categories` key. Refused with nothing on either stream: the four non-string values of (1). TWELVE THINGS THE CAPTURE ITSELF EXPOSED, each pinned by a case rather than by a sentence. (1) D1. A non-string category value makes resolve-models exit 5 with EMPTY stdout and EMPTY stderr -- rm-valor-true-cc, rm-valor-numero-cc, rm-valor-objeto-cc, rm-valor-array-cc -- violating its own documented contract that stdout is always valid JSON and every failure path returns the fallback at exit 0. Three things compound: jq's `//` fires only on null and false, so a non-string survives into the "INVALID\t" + value concatenation, which is a type error; that jq call's stderr is discarded with no || fallback, unlike the two before it; and it is a BARE assignment to an already-declared local, so under `set -euo pipefail` jq's status takes the whole shell down. It is host-conditional, which is the tell: with an EMPTY valid set the validation pass never runs and the same config prints {"research":true,...} at exit 0 -- rm-valor-true-oc-sem-binario. Captured as-is and ported to as-is; the repair is its own commit, and it has landed: the six entries above -- rm-valor-true-cc, rm-valor-numero-cc, rm-valor-objeto-cc, rm-valor-array-cc, rm-valor-numero-oc-stub and rm-valor-true-oc-stub -- were the ONLY records edited after capture, in the commit that changed the rule, and each now holds exit 0, the all-but-research result, and one warning naming the value in the compact JSON form jq's own string interpolation would have used. What they recorded before is in this file's history and in that commit's diff. Everything else here is still the bash's. (2) `false` and `null` both resolve to inherit while `0` does not -- rm-valor-false-cc and rm-valor-null-cc against rm-valor-numero-cc -- because `//` reads false as absent and 0 as present. models-prompt-check inherits the same asymmetry from its own `//`: mpc-valor-zero-cc answers skip and mpc-valor-false-cc answers prompt. (3) Malformed JSON is reported as "schema 1.0 obsoleto" -- rm-json-malformado-cc, gcm-json-malformado-cc -- because jq's parse failure lands in the `|| _schema_ok="reject"` handler on the schema pass. The documented "malformed JSON or failed to parse" message is reachable only when the file PARSES and `.categories`, or its host sub-table, is not an object: rm-categories-string-cc, rm-categories-host-string-cc, rm-categories-host-array-oc-stub. Both messages name the config path. (4) D4. One invalid id containing a newline produces TWO warnings, and the second names a category that does not exist while claiming an empty model id -- rm-id-com-newline-cc on Claude Code, rm-id-com-newline-oc-stub on OpenCode, where the fabricated category is a model id. The `while IFS=$'\t' read -r _cat _val` loop is line-oriented and the value it reads is not. (5) An INTERNAL tab survives the same loop intact, single or doubled -- rm-id-com-tab-cc, rm-id-com-tab-duplo-cc, rm-id-com-tab-oc-stub -- because `read` hands the whole remainder after the FIRST delimiter to the last variable, verbatim. The delimiter's only real casualty is the newline, so changing the delimiter a third time would have fixed nothing. (6) resolve-models emits the NORMALIZED id, not the stored one: a config holding "  sonnet  " resolves to "sonnet" -- rm-id-espaco-nas-pontas-cc, rm-id-espaco-nas-pontas-oc-stub -- while get-current-models, which does not validate, hands the padded string straight back (gcm-id-espaco-nas-pontas-cc). (7) jq reads a STREAM, not one value. A two-document models.json runs the verb twice and prints two lines of JSON -- rm-dois-documentos-cc, gcm-dois-documentos-cc -- and the same shape makes models-prompt-check answer prompt for a file whose single document would have answered skip (mpc-dois-documentos-cc), because the bash compares jq's whole multi-line output against the literal "true". (8) A whitespace-only file lands in resolve-models' "empty result" branch WITH a warning (rm-so-espacos-cc) and in get-current-models' equivalent branch with NO warning at all (gcm-so-espacos-cc). The two verbs' last-resort branches differ by exactly one line to stderr, and both are contract. (9) D10, recorded and deliberately carried across unchanged. The OpenCode cache is keyed on the mtime of models.json but its VALUE is the output of `opencode models`: a seeded cache beats the live binary (rm-cache-preexistente-vence-oc, lm-oc-cache-preexistente) and is not consulted at all when the binary is absent, because the `command -v opencode` probe returns first (rm-cache-preexistente-ignorado-sem-binario-oc). No case anywhere deletes one. Fixing the key would change WHEN a shell-out happens, which is a behaviour change and cannot ride inside a delta-zero commit. (10) list-models normalizes what it OFFERS -- padded entries trimmed, empty entries dropped (lm-oc-cache-preexistente) -- and falls back to the built-in Anthropic list whenever the set is empty for either of its two reasons: no binary (lm-oc-sem-binario) or a binary that printed nothing (lm-oc-stub-vazio). Its Claude Code branch reads no config at all and answers the same three aliases with or without one (lm-cc, lm-cc-sem-config). (11) The two JSON output spellings coexist and are both contract: resolve-models and get-current-models print COMPACT single-line objects, list-models prints a PRETTY two-space-indented array. (12) The `python3` cases record what a python3-less host sees TODAY, which is everything -- these four verbs are pure bash and jq at this commit, so hiding the interpreter changes nothing. They are here so the port's degrade path is measured against a real before-state instead of an assumption. The ones the port deliberately changes are named, with what each costs, in test_models.py's KNOWN_DIVERGENCES; the recording itself is never edited to match the port.
